entities.summary:
The Siege of Leningrad was a pivotal 872-day blockade of the Soviet city of Leningrad (modern-day Saint Petersburg) by German and Finnish forces during World War II. It began on September 8, 1941, and lasted until January 27, 1944. The siege was one of the longest and most devastating in modern history, with over 1.5 million civilians and military personnel estimated to have perished.

The blockade had a significant impact on the Soviet war effort, with the city's defenders facing extreme hardship and the Soviet government struggling to maintain supplies. Despite this, the Soviet army managed to hold off the German and Finnish forces, and the city was eventually relieved in 1944. The siege is remembered as a testament to the resilience of the Soviet people and a grim reminder of the human cost of war.

The Siege of Leningrad also had a profound impact on the course of World War II, with the Soviet Union's ability to maintain a significant military presence on the Eastern Front a crucial factor in the ultimate defeat of Nazi Germany. The siege is also seen as a turning point in the development of Soviet culture and identity, with the city's experience of hardship and sacrifice becoming a powerful symbol of national resilience.

As Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev later noted, 'The people of Leningrad proved themselves worthy of the great traditions of the Russian people.' The city's experience during the siege remains a powerful reminder of the human cost of war and the importance of resilience and determination in the face of adversity.
